title: Ratio and Proportion Grade 5: Ratios, Equivalent Ratios & the Unitary Method + Free Quiz
meta_title: Ratio and Proportion Grade 5 (Simple Guide) + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Learn ratio and proportion grade 5: write and simplify ratios, find equivalent ratios and use the unitary method, with a free quiz and worksheet.
excerpt: A ratio is just a comparison — 2 cups of rice to 3 cups of water. Here is how I introduce ratio, equivalent ratios and simple proportion to Grade 5, with kitchen and shopping examples and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Picture a Grade 5 child helping in the kitchen. The recipe says 2 cups of rice to 3 cups of water. That single line — 2 to 3 — is ratio and proportion grade 5 in a nutshell. A ratio compares two amounts; a proportion keeps that comparison the same when you scale up or down. Get this idea clear now and the child walks into Grade 6 percentages, speed and unit-rate problems already halfway there.

The mistake I see most often is teaching ratio as a fraction to be calculated rather than a comparison to be understood. So before any symbols, I want the child to say the words out loud: ‘for every 2 cups of rice, 3 cups of water.’ Once that sentence is natural, the notation is easy.

What a ratio actually means

A ratio compares quantities of the same kind. We write it with a colon: 2 cups to 3 cups becomes 2 : 3, read as ‘two to three.’ Order matters. The ratio of boys to girls is not the same as girls to boys, so 8 : 12 and 12 : 8 describe two different situations.

Two quick rules I drill early:

  • Both quantities must be in the same unit before you compare. To compare 1 metre with 50 cm, change the metre to 100 cm first, then write 100 : 50.
  • A ratio has no units of its own. 100 cm : 50 cm simplifies to 2 : 1 — just two bare numbers.

Writing and simplifying ratios

Simplifying a ratio works exactly like simplifying a fraction: divide both parts by their highest common factor. If a fruit basket has 8 apples and 12 oranges, the ratio of apples to oranges is 8 : 12. Divide both by 4 and you get 2 : 3 — the simplest form. Same relationship, smaller numbers.

A common slip

Children sometimes divide only one side, turning 8 : 12 into 2 : 12. Whatever you do to the first number, you must do to the second. I tell them a ratio is a see-saw: keep it balanced or it tips over.

Equivalent ratios

Equivalent ratios are ratios that describe the same comparison. Multiply or divide both parts by the same number and the ratio stays true. Starting from 2 : 3, I can build a whole family: 4 : 6, 6 : 9, 8 : 12, 20 : 30. Every one of them still means ‘for every 2 of the first, 3 of the second.’

This is the single most useful idea in the whole topic, because it is the bridge to proportion. A neat classroom trick: write the ratio as a fraction and ask the child to find equal fractions. It connects two things they already know.

Simple proportion and the unitary method

When two ratios are equal, they form a proportion. If 2 cups of rice need 3 cups of water, then 4 cups of rice need 6 cups — because 2 : 3 = 4 : 6. That is a proportion in action.

For most real problems the cleanest tool is the unitary method: first find the value of one, then multiply for many. Suppose 4 notebooks cost ₹60. Find the cost of one (60 ÷ 4 = ₹15), then the cost of any number (7 notebooks = 15 × 7 = ₹105). Find one, then scale — that is the whole method.

4 pens cost ₹2020 ÷ 4 = ₹56 pens = 5 × 6 = ₹30
3 kg rice cost ₹135135 ÷ 3 = ₹455 kg = 45 × 5 = ₹225
5 laddoos cost ₹5050 ÷ 5 = ₹108 laddoos = 10 × 8 = ₹80

Practising at the sabzi mandi

The vegetable market is the best free worksheet a parent has. If tomatoes are ₹40 for 2 kg, ask your child what 3 kg would cost before the vendor does the sum. If a shopkeeper mixes 1 scoop of squash with 4 scoops of water, ask how much water 3 scoops of squash need. These are proportion problems wearing everyday clothes.

One honest caveat. Do not rush a Grade 5 child into cross-multiplication or the ‘means and extremes’ shortcut. That is a Grade 6 formalisation. At this stage the unitary method is slower but it builds real understanding, and understanding is what carries forward. Speed can wait.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz covering exactly what we have looked at — writing ratios, simplifying, equivalent ratios and the unitary method. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they want longer graded practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives plenty of questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 5 Ratio and Proportion Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on writing ratios, simplifying, equivalent ratios and the unitary method. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 5 ratio, equivalent ratios and simple proportion

questions.q: Simplify the ratio 4 : 6 to its lowest terms.
questions.explanation: Divide both parts by their highest common factor, 2. So 4 becomes 2 and 6 becomes 3, giving 2 : 3.
Multiply both parts by 2: 1 becomes 2 and 3 becomes 6, so 2 : 6 is equivalent to 1 : 3.

questions.q: A recipe uses 2 cups of rice to 3 cups of water. For 4 cups of rice, how much water is needed?
questions.explanation: The rice doubled from 2 to 4, so double the water too: 3 becomes 6. The proportion is 2 : 3 = 4 : 6.

questions.q: If 3 pencils cost ₹15, what is the cost of one pencil?
questions.explanation: Use the unitary method: find the cost of one by dividing. 15 ÷ 3 = ₹5.

questions.q: Using the price above, what do 7 pencils cost?
questions.explanation: One pencil costs ₹5, so seven cost 5 × 7 = ₹35.

questions.q: A class of 20 has 8 boys and 12 girls. The ratio of boys to girls in simplest form is:
questions.explanation: Divide both parts by 4: 8 becomes 2 and 12 becomes 3, giving 2 : 3.

questions.q: What does the ratio 5 : 2 tell you?
options: For every 5 of the first there are 2 of the second
questions.explanation: A ratio is a comparison: 5 : 2 means for every 5 parts of the first quantity there are 2 parts of the second.

questions.q: Two ratios that are equal to each other form a:
questions.explanation: When two ratios are equal, such as 2 : 3 = 4 : 6, together they form a proportion.

faq.q: What is the difference between a ratio and a proportion?
faq.a: A ratio compares two quantities, like 2 : 3. A proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal, like 2 : 3 = 4 : 6. In short, a proportion is made of two matching ratios.

faq.q: Do both parts of a ratio need the same unit?
faq.a: Yes. Convert to the same unit first, then compare. To compare 1 metre with 50 cm, change the metre to 100 cm, write 100 : 50, and simplify to 2 : 1. A ratio itself carries no unit.

faq.q: What is the unitary method in Grade 5?
faq.a: Find the value of one item, then multiply for the number you want. If 4 notebooks cost ₹60, one costs 60 ÷ 4 = ₹15, so 7 notebooks cost 15 × 7 = ₹105. Find one, then scale up.

faq.q: Should a Grade 5 child learn cross-multiplication?
faq.a: Not yet. Cross-multiplication is usually introduced in Grade 6. At Grade 5 the unitary method builds stronger understanding, even though it takes an extra step, and that understanding carries forward.
